items.stem: Which of the following best describes "geostationary orbit"?
options: A human-made object placed in orbit, e.g. for communications or weather
The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m
An orbit above the equator with a period of 24 hours, so the satellite stays above the same point on Earth
The recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance: v = H₀d
items.answer: An orbit above the equator with a period of 24 hours, so the satellite stays above the same point on Earth
items.markingKey: C. "geostationary orbit" is an orbit above the equator with a period of 24 hours, so the satellite stays above the same point on Earth.

items.stem: Explain why the speed of a comet changes during its elliptical orbit.
items.answer: Near the Sun gravity is stronger and the comet speeds up as it falls inward; far from the Sun it slows down as it moves outward against gravity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Near the Sun gravity is stronger and the comet speeds up as it falls inward; far from the Sun it slows down as it moves outward against gravity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Planets orbit the Sun in perfect circles." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Planetary orbits are ellipses, though most are close to circular.
items.markingKey: Planetary orbits are ellipses, though most are close to circular. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Nia is investigating how the radius of a circular path affects the time period of a bung whirled on a string, as a model of orbits. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the radius increases, then the period will increase, because with the same central force the bung must move more slowly around a longer path.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the radius increases, then the period will increase, because with the same central force the bung must move more slowly around a longer path.

items.stem: The orbital radius of a geostationary satellite is 4.22 × 10^7 m and its period is 23.93 hours. Calculate its orbital speed in m/s.
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Companies should be allowed to launch unlimited numbers of satellites for internet coverage."
items.answer: Large constellations need international regulation of numbers, brightness and end-of-life disposal.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: brings internet to remote regions; commercial investment drives innovation. Arguments against: increases space debris and collision risk; bright satellites interfere with astronomy. Supported judgement: Large constellations need international regulation of numbers, brightness and end-of-life disposal.

items.stem: How does the orbital period of a planet change with distance from the Sun?
options: Planets further away take longer to orbit
items.answer: Planets further away take longer to orbit
items.markingKey: A. Weaker gravity and longer path.

items.stem: Explain why a satellite in a stable orbit does not fall to Earth.
items.answer: It is falling towards Earth all the time, but its sideways speed is so high that the Earth’s surface curves away as fast as it falls, so it keeps going round.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is falling towards Earth all the time, but its sideways speed is so high that the Earth’s surface curves away as fast as it falls, so it keeps going round. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a low polar orbit and a geostationary orbit.
items.answer: A geostationary orbit is high (about 36 000 km), above the equator, with a 24-hour period; a low polar orbit is a few hundred kilometres up, passes over the poles and has a period of about 100 minutes.
items.markingKey: A geostationary orbit is high (about 36 000 km), above the equator, with a 24-hour period; a low polar orbit is a few hundred kilometres up, passes over the poles and has a period of about 100 minutes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a dwarf planet and a planet.
items.answer: A planet orbits the Sun, is round and has cleared its orbit of other objects; a dwarf planet is round but has not cleared its orbit.
items.markingKey: A planet orbits the Sun, is round and has cleared its orbit of other objects; a dwarf planet is round but has not cleared its orbit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Space debris as an example, explain artificial satellites and their impacts.
items.answer: Over 30 000 tracked pieces of debris orbit Earth; collisions (e.g. Iridium–Cosmos 2009) create more fragments. Debris threatens satellites and astronauts and raises questions about responsibility for clean-up.
items.markingKey: Context (Over 30 000 tracked pieces of debris orbit Earth; collisions (e.g. Iridium–Cosmos 2009) create more fragments.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Debris threatens satellites and astronauts and raises questions about responsibility for clean-up. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to artificial satellites and their impacts.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the radius of a circular path affects the time period of a bung whirled on a string, as a model of orbits. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): wear eye protection; check the bung is tied securely; clear space around the student. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. wear eye protection; check the bung is tied securely; clear space around the student); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Describe how gravity keeps planets and satellites in orbit, explain how orbital speed and period change with orbital radius, and compare geostationary and polar orbits for different uses.
items.answer: Gravity provides a centripetal force towards the central body; the body’s velocity is tangential, so it continuously changes direction. Larger radius → weaker gravity → lower speed and longer period (T² ∝ r³). Geostationary: 24 h, equatorial, ~36 000 km – communications, TV. Polar: low, ~100 min – mapping, weather, spying; scans whole Earth.
items.markingKey: Gravity provides a centripetal force towards the central body; the body’s velocity is tangential, so it continuously changes direction. Larger radius → weaker gravity → lower speed and longer period (T² ∝ r³). Geostationary: 24 h, equatorial, ~36 000 km – communications, TV. Polar: low, ~100 min – mapping, weather, spying; scans whole Earth.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The extremely dense remnant of a supernova, made mostly of neutrons"?
items.answer: neutron star
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of neutron star.

items.stem: A student claims: "Stars burn hydrogen like a fire." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Stars release energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei, not by chemical burning with oxygen.
items.markingKey: Stars release energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei, not by chemical burning with oxygen. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a star leaves the main sequence.
items.answer: The hydrogen in its core runs low, so fusion slows, the core contracts and heats, and the outer layers expand – it becomes a red giant (or supergiant). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The hydrogen in its core runs low, so fusion slows, the core contracts and heats, and the outer layers expand – it becomes a red giant (or supergiant). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which Supernova 1987A shows supernovae.
items.answer: A supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud was seen with the naked eye; neutrino detectors recorded the burst hours before the light arrived. Confirmed models of core collapse in massive stars.
items.markingKey: Context (A supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud was seen with the naked eye; neutrino detectors recorded the burst hours before the light arrived.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Confirmed models of core collapse in massive stars. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to supernovae.

items.stem: A star’s main-sequence lifetime is roughly t = 10 × M^(−2.5) billion years, where M is its mass in solar masses. Estimate the lifetime of a star of 0.5 solar masses, and explain why massive stars live shorter lives.
items.answer: about 56.6 billion years
items.markingKey: M1 t = 10 × 0.5^(−2.5); A1 ≈ 56.6 billion years; B1 massive stars have stronger gravity, hotter cores and fuse hydrogen much faster.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "“We are made of star stuff” (Carl Sagan) is scientifically accurate."
items.answer: Mostly accurate: almost all elements heavier than helium in our bodies were made in stars.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and iron were made by fusion in stars; supernovae scattered these elements into the gas that formed the solar system. Arguments against: hydrogen in our bodies was made in the Big Bang, not in stars; some light elements come from other processes. Supported judgement: Mostly accurate: almost all elements heavier than helium in our bodies were made in stars.

items.stem: Define the term "neutron star".
items.answer: The extremely dense remnant of a supernova, made mostly of neutrons
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the extremely dense remnant of a supernova, made mostly of neutrons. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between the life cycle of a Sun-like star and the life cycle of a massive star.
items.answer: A Sun-like star becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf; a massive star becomes a red supergiant, explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star or black hole.
items.markingKey: A Sun-like star becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf; a massive star becomes a red supergiant, explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star or black hole. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the iron in your blood was made inside stars.
items.answer: Elements up to iron are made by fusion in the cores of massive stars; these were scattered by supernovae and became part of the cloud that formed the Sun and Earth.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Elements up to iron are made by fusion in the cores of massive stars; these were scattered by supernovae and became part of the cloud that formed the Sun and Earth. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Isabel used published data for main-sequence stars to compare mass with estimated lifetime.

Mass of star / solar masses | Main-sequence lifetime / billion years: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.8 | 19.51 | 18.78 | 18.93
1.0 | 10.66 | 11.02 | 10.61
1.5 | 3.92 | 4.12 | 3.94
2.0 | 1.87 | 1.89 | 1.88
3.0 | 0.70 | 0.70 | 0.72

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The lifetime falls steeply as the mass of the star increases. A more massive star has stronger gravity, so its core is hotter and denser and fuses hydrogen much faster; it uses up its fuel sooner even though it has more of it.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The lifetime falls steeply as the mass of the star increases.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: A more massive star has stronger gravity, so its core is hotter and denser and fuses hydrogen much faster; it uses up its fuel sooner even though it has more of it.

items.stem: Ingrid plans to investigate how the temperature of a glowing filament affects its colour, as a model for star colour and temperature. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: the same lamp; the same distance from lamp to sensor; a darkened room; the same filters and sensor

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the temperature of a glowing filament affects its colour, as a model for star colour and temperature. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Connect the lamp to a variable supply and measure the voltage; fix a light sensor 20 cm away in a dark box; for each voltage take readings through a red then a blue filter; repeat three times; calculate the red:blue ratio and plot it against voltage.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (the lamp gets very hot; do not touch it; keep below the rated voltage). Model: Connect the lamp to a variable supply and measure the voltage; fix a light sensor 20 cm away in a dark box; for each voltage take readings through a red then a blue filter; repeat three times; calculate the red:blue ratio and plot it against voltage.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The theory that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since"?
items.answer: Big Bang theory
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Big Bang theory.

items.stem: Explain how red-shift shows that the universe is expanding.
items.answer: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, showing they are moving away; the further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift, so space itself is expanding in all directions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, showing they are moving away; the further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift, so space itself is expanding in all directions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Big Bang theory and the steady-state theory.
items.answer: The Big Bang theory says the universe began in a hot, dense state and is expanding and cooling; the steady-state theory said the universe has always existed, with new matter created as it expands, keeping density constant.
items.markingKey: The Big Bang theory says the universe began in a hot, dense state and is expanding and cooling; the steady-state theory said the universe has always existed, with new matter created as it expands, keeping density constant. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Discovery of the CMB (1964) shows evidence for the Big Bang.
items.answer: Penzias and Wilson found unexplained microwave “noise” from all directions in their radio antenna. An accidental discovery that matched predictions and led to the Nobel Prize in 1978.
items.markingKey: Context (Penzias and Wilson found unexplained microwave “noise” from all directions in their radio antenna.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: An accidental discovery that matched predictions and led to the Nobel Prize in 1978. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evidence for the Big Bang.

items.stem: The age of the universe can be estimated as 1/H₀. If H₀ = 67 km/s/Mpc, then 1/H₀ = 977.8 ÷ 67 billion years. Calculate the estimated age and explain why different values of H₀ give different ages.
items.answer: about 14.6 billion years
items.markingKey: M1 977.8 ÷ 67; A1 ≈ 14.6 billion years; B1 larger H₀ → faster expansion → less time needed to reach present size, so a younger universe.

items.stem: Felix plans an investigation into how the distance between dots on an inflating balloon affects how fast they move apart, as a model of Hubble’s law. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (initial distance of dots from a reference dot (2, 4, 6, 8, 10 cm)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which observation is strong evidence for the Big Bang and not for a steady-state universe?
items.answer: The cosmic microwave background radiation
items.markingKey: D. Predicted remnant of the hot early universe.

items.stem: "Red-shift means a galaxy looks red to the eye." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Red-shift means spectral lines are shifted to longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red.
items.markingKey: Red-shift means spectral lines are shifted to longer wavelengths; the galaxy need not appear red. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The Big Bang was an explosion at a particular point in space." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The Big Bang was the expansion of space itself everywhere, not an explosion into existing space from a centre.
items.markingKey: The Big Bang was the expansion of space itself everywhere, not an explosion into existing space from a centre. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the distance between dots on an inflating balloon affects how fast they move apart, as a model of Hubble’s law, state the dependent variable and describe how Amara should measure it.
items.answer: increase in distance from the reference dot after a set number of pumps
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: increase in distance from the reference dot after a set number of pumps.

items.stem: "The Big Bang theory is proven beyond doubt." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The Big Bang is the best-supported model, but science never proves theories absolutely and details are still being refined.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: red-shift, CMB and the abundance of light elements all support it; it makes successful predictions. Arguments against: dark matter and dark energy are not yet understood; the Hubble tension shows measurements disagree. Supported judgement: The Big Bang is the best-supported model, but science never proves theories absolutely and details are still being refined. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Explain what red-shift is and how observations of red-shift and the cosmic microwave background support the Big Bang theory. Discuss why scientific ideas about the origin of the universe have changed over time.
items.answer: Red-shift: absorption lines from distant galaxies shifted to longer wavelengths → galaxies receding. Greater distance → greater red-shift (Hubble’s law) → expanding universe → traced back to a single hot, dense origin. CMB: uniform microwave radiation from all directions, predicted as cooled radiation from early universe; steady-state could not explain it. Change: static universe → expanding (Hubble) → Big Bang vs steady state → Big Bang accepted after CMB; ongoing work on dark energy. Theories change with new evidence and technology.
items.markingKey: Red-shift: absorption lines from distant galaxies shifted to longer wavelengths → galaxies receding. Greater distance → greater red-shift (Hubble’s law) → expanding universe → traced back to a single hot, dense origin. CMB: uniform microwave radiation from all directions, predicted as cooled radiation from early universe; steady-state could not explain it. Change: static universe → expanding (Hubble) → Big Bang vs steady state → Big Bang accepted after CMB; ongoing work on dark energy. Theories change with new evidence and technology.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "space probe"?

The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m

items.markingKey: C. "space probe" is an uncrewed spacecraft sent to study other bodies in the solar system.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Space telescopes are used because they are closer to the stars." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The extra distance of a few hundred kilometres is negligible; they are used to get above the atmosphere.
items.markingKey: The extra distance of a few hundred kilometres is negligible; they are used to get above the atmosphere. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: 1076 times

items.stem: Compare ground-based and space telescopes, explaining how the choice depends on the wavelength being observed, and evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of a major space mission such as the James Webb Space Telescope.
items.answer: Atmosphere absorbs gamma, X-ray, most UV and IR → those need space telescopes; visible and radio reach the ground. Ground: large, cheap, maintainable; but turbulence, weather, light pollution. Space: sharp images, all wavelengths; but very expensive, no repair (JWST at L2), limited lifetime. JWST: infrared shows the earliest galaxies (red-shifted), star formation behind dust, exoplanet atmospheres; cost ~$10 billion, delays, risk of failure. Judgement weighing scientific return against cost.

items.answer: A space telescope avoids atmospheric absorption and blurring but is expensive and hard to repair; a ground-based telescope can be larger, cheaper and upgraded but is limited by the atmosphere and weather.
items.markingKey: A space telescope avoids atmospheric absorption and blurring but is expensive and hard to repair; a ground-based telescope can be larger, cheaper and upgraded but is limited by the atmosphere and weather. items.markingKey: Gravity at the ISS is about 90% of that on the surface; astronauts float because they and the station are in free fall together. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a neutron star and a white dwarf.
items.answer: A white dwarf is the remnant of a Sun-like star, about Earth-sized and held up by electron pressure; a neutron star forms in a supernova of a massive star, is only about 20 km across and is made of neutrons.
items.markingKey: A white dwarf is the remnant of a Sun-like star, about Earth-sized and held up by electron pressure; a neutron star forms in a supernova of a massive star, is only about 20 km across and is made of neutrons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the Big Bang theory and the steady-state theory.
items.answer: The Big Bang theory says the universe began in a hot, dense state and is expanding and cooling; the steady-state theory said the universe has always existed, with new matter created as it expands, keeping density constant.
items.markingKey: The Big Bang theory says the universe began in a hot, dense state and is expanding and cooling; the steady-state theory said the universe has always existed, with new matter created as it expands, keeping density constant. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Telescopes work mainly by making things look bigger." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Their main job is to collect more radiation (light-gathering power) and to resolve fine detail.
items.markingKey: Their main job is to collect more radiation (light-gathering power) and to resolve fine detail. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a geostationary orbit and a low polar orbit.
items.answer: A geostationary orbit is high (about 36 000 km), above the equator, with a 24-hour period; a low polar orbit is a few hundred kilometres up, passes over the poles and has a period of about 100 minutes.
items.markingKey: A geostationary orbit is high (about 36 000 km), above the equator, with a 24-hour period; a low polar orbit is a few hundred kilometres up, passes over the poles and has a period of about 100 minutes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the temperature of a glowing filament affects its colour, as a model for star colour and temperature, state the dependent variable and describe how Freya should measure it.
items.answer: ratio of red to blue light intensity measured with a light sensor and coloured filters
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: ratio of red to blue light intensity measured with a light sensor and coloured filters.

items.stem: Briefly describe Discovery of the CMB (1964) and explain what it reveals about evidence for the Big Bang.
items.answer: Penzias and Wilson found unexplained microwave “noise” from all directions in their radio antenna. An accidental discovery that matched predictions and led to the Nobel Prize in 1978.

items.stem: Describe the life cycle of a star with a mass much greater than the Sun, explaining the role of gravity and fusion at each stage, and compare it with the life cycle of the Sun.
items.answer: Nebula collapses under gravity → protostar heats → fusion of H begins → main sequence (fusion pressure balances gravity). Massive star: H runs out → red supergiant, fuses heavier elements up to iron → core collapses → supernova → neutron star or black hole. Sun: main sequence ~10 billion years → red giant → sheds planetary nebula → white dwarf. Massive stars live shorter lives and make heavy elements.
items.markingKey: Nebula collapses under gravity → protostar heats → fusion of H begins → main sequence (fusion pressure balances gravity). Massive star: H runs out → red supergiant, fuses heavier elements up to iron → core collapses → supernova → neutron star or black hole. Sun: main sequence ~10 billion years → red giant → sheds planetary nebula → white dwarf. Massive stars live shorter lives and make heavy elements.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The Big Bang theory is proven beyond doubt."
items.answer: The Big Bang is the best-supported model, but science never proves theories absolutely and details are still being refined.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: red-shift, CMB and the abundance of light elements all support it; it makes successful predictions. Arguments against: dark matter and dark energy are not yet understood; the Hubble tension shows measurements disagree. Supported judgement: The Big Bang is the best-supported model, but science never proves theories absolutely and details are still being refined. items.stem: "Humans, not robots, should be sent to explore Mars." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Robots are better value for most science now; human missions may follow once the risks are reduced.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: humans can adapt and make decisions quickly; inspires the public. Arguments against: far more expensive and risky; radiation and long journeys; robots can work for years without life support. Supported judgement: Robots are better value for most science now; human missions may follow once the risks are reduced. items.stem: What will the Sun eventually become?
options: A red giant, then a white dwarf
A supernova, then a black hole
items.answer: A red giant, then a white dwarf
items.markingKey: B. The Sun is not massive enough for a supernova.

items.stem: Why is the CMB now detected as microwaves rather than visible light or gamma rays?
items.answer: The expansion of the universe has stretched its wavelength

items.stem: Explain the difference between a reflecting telescope and a refracting telescope.
items.answer: A reflecting telescope uses a curved mirror and can be built very large; a refracting telescope uses lenses, which sag and cause colour fringes when very large.
items.markingKey: A reflecting telescope uses a curved mirror and can be built very large; a refracting telescope uses lenses, which sag and cause colour fringes when very large. items.stem: Diego writes: "Planets orbit the Sun in perfect circles." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Planetary orbits are ellipses, though most are close to circular.
items.markingKey: Planetary orbits are ellipses, though most are close to circular. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Zara writes: "Black holes suck in everything in the universe." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Far from a black hole its gravity is like that of any object of the same mass; only matter that comes close is captured.
items.markingKey: Far from a black hole its gravity is like that of any object of the same mass; only matter that comes close is captured. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the age of the universe can be estimated from Hubble’s constant.
items.answer: If galaxies have been moving apart at speed v from a single point, the time taken to reach distance d is d/v = 1/H₀, which gives an estimate of the time since the Big Bang.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Kepler’s laws (1609–1619) shows orbital patterns.
items.answer: Using Tycho Brahe’s data, Kepler showed planets move in ellipses and that T² is proportional to r³. Newton later explained the laws with his law of gravitation.

items.stem:
Aiko used published data for main-sequence stars to compare mass with estimated lifetime.

Mass of star / solar masses | Main-sequence lifetime / billion years: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.8 | 16.71 | 17.80 | 17.45
1.0 | 9.83 | 9.91 | 9.49
1.5 | 3.72 | 3.52 | 3.67
2.0 | 1.73 | 1.72 | 1.76
3.0 | 0.62 | 0.65 | 0.62

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The lifetime falls steeply as the mass of the star increases. A more massive star has stronger gravity, so its core is hotter and denser and fuses hydrogen much faster; it uses up its fuel sooner even though it has more of it.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the radius of a circular path affects the time period of a bung whirled on a string, as a model of orbits. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Thread a string through a glass tube; tie a rubber bung to one end and a 100 g mass to the other; mark the radius with a paper clip; whirl the bung so the clip stays just below the tube; time 10 revolutions; repeat three times for each radius; calculate T and plot T² against r.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (wear eye protection; check the bung is tied securely; clear space around the student). items.stem: "“We are made of star stuff” (Carl Sagan) is scientifically accurate." Discuss.
items.answer: Mostly accurate: almost all elements heavier than helium in our bodies were made in stars.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and iron were made by fusion in stars; supernovae scattered these elements into the gas that formed the solar system. Arguments against: hydrogen in our bodies was made in the Big Bang, not in stars; some light elements come from other processes. Supported judgement: Mostly accurate: almost all elements heavier than helium in our bodies were made in stars. items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the diameter of a lens aperture affects the ability to resolve two close light sources, as a model of telescope resolution. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Fix two red LEDs 2 mm apart at the end of a corridor; view them through a lens covered by a card mask with a hole; walk back until they merge into one; measure the distance; repeat with each aperture and three observers; plot maximum distance against aperture.

Model: Fix two red LEDs 2 mm apart at the end of a corridor; view them through a lens covered by a card mask with a hole; walk back until they merge into one; measure the distance; repeat with each aperture and three observers; plot maximum distance against aperture.
